questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Lung: COPD, pneumonia, carcinoma lung, occupational lung disease
questions.stem: Which lung carcinoma is most strongly associated with smoking and characteristically arises centrally with cavitation and hypercalcaemia?
options: Squamous cell carcinoma, secreting parathyroid hormone-related peptide
questions.concept: Adenocarcinoma is now the commonest overall and the commonest in non-smokers and in women, arising peripherally and carrying targetable EGFR and ALK alterations.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. The Lung

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Lung: COPD, pneumonia, carcinoma lung, occupational lung disease
questions.stem: Which occupational exposure causes upper zone nodular fibrosis with eggshell calcification of hilar nodes and a greatly increased risk of tuberculosis?
questions.concept: Silica impairs macrophage function, which explains the tuberculosis association, whereas asbestos causes lower zone fibrosis with pleural plaques and mesothelioma.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. The Lung

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Lung: COPD, pneumonia, carcinoma lung, occupational lung disease
questions.stem: Which pathological definition distinguishes emphysema from chronic bronchitis?
options: Emphysema is permanent alveolar enlargement with wall destruction, while chronic bronchitis is defined clinically by productive cough for 3 months in 2 consecutive years
questions.concept: Because one definition is anatomical and the other clinical, the two frequently coexist, and the Reid index of gland to wall thickness is the histological correlate of bronchitis.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. The Lung

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Lung: COPD, pneumonia, carcinoma lung, occupational lung disease
questions.stem: Which paraneoplastic syndrome is characteristic of small cell carcinoma of the lung?
options: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion and ectopic ACTH production
questions.concept: Its neuroendocrine origin explains the hormonal syndromes and the Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, and it is almost always disseminated at presentation so it is treated with chemotherapy rather than surgery.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. The Lung

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Lung: COPD, pneumonia, carcinoma lung, occupational lung disease
questions.stem: Which type of emphysema is associated with alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, and which with smoking?
options: Panacinar emphysema affecting the lower lobes in deficiency, and centriacinar emphysema affecting the upper lobes in smoking
Centriacinar in deficiency and panacinar in smoking
questions.concept: Unopposed neutrophil elastase in deficiency destroys the whole acinus and the basal distribution reflects greater perfusion, whereas smoke deposition is greatest in the upper zone respiratory bronchioles.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. The Lung

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Lung: COPD, pneumonia, carcinoma lung, occupational lung disease
questions.stem: Why does asbestos exposure multiply the risk of bronchogenic carcinoma in a smoker far more than either exposure alone?
options: The two carcinogens act synergistically on the same bronchial epithelium, so the combined risk is multiplicative rather than additive
questions.concept: Mesothelioma risk by contrast is not increased by smoking, which is why the two asbestos-related malignancies behave differently in relation to tobacco.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. The Lung

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which testicular germ cell tumour is most common, radiosensitive and associated with a raised placental alkaline phosphatase?
questions.concept: Alpha-fetoprotein elevation excludes pure seminoma and indicates a non-seminomatous element, which changes both prognosis and management.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. The Male and Female Genital Tracts

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which human papillomavirus types account for most cervical carcinoma, and which viral proteins are responsible?
options: Types 16 and 18, through E6 degrading p53 and E7 inactivating RB
Types 6 and 11, through E1 and E2
Types 16 and 18, through L1 capsid protein
questions.concept: Types 6 and 11 cause condylomata rather than cancer, and vaccine design targets the L1 capsid protein because it generates neutralising antibody.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. The Male and Female Genital Tracts

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which prostatic zone gives rise to most carcinomas, and which to benign hyperplasia?
options: The peripheral zone for carcinoma and the transitional zone for hyperplasia
The anterior fibromuscular stroma for carcinoma
questions.concept: This anatomy explains why carcinoma is palpable on digital rectal examination while hyperplasia obstructs the urethra, and why they can coexist independently.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. The Male and Female Genital Tracts

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which grading system is used for prostatic adenocarcinoma, and what does it assess?
options: The Gleason system, based on the architectural pattern of glands rather than nuclear features
The Fuhrman system, based on nuclear grade
questions.concept: Because it is architectural, it is assessed at low power, and the modern grade group system translates Gleason scores into five prognostic groups to improve communication.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. The Male and Female Genital Tracts

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which ovarian tumour contains mature tissue from more than one germ layer and is the commonest ovarian neoplasm in young women?
options: Mature cystic teratoma, or dermoid cyst
questions.concept: Malignant transformation is rare and usually squamous, and the specific risk of torsion together with the rare complication of gliomatosis peritonei and of anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis are worth knowing.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. The Male and Female Genital Tracts

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Why does testicular carcinoma in situ warrant treatment even though it is confined to the seminiferous tubules?
options: It progresses to invasive germ cell tumour in the great majority within a few years
It is not a precursor lesion
questions.concept: It is often found in the contralateral testis of a man with a germ cell tumour and in biopsy of an atrophic or undescended testis, so its identification alters surveillance and treatment of the remaining gonad.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. The Male and Female Genital Tracts

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which finding in the marrow defines a myelodysplastic syndrome?
options: Dysplastic maturation of one or more lineages with ineffective haemopoiesis and cytopenias, with fewer than 20 percent blasts
questions.concept: The paradox of a cellular marrow with peripheral cytopenias reflects intramedullary apoptosis, and the risk of transformation to acute myeloid leukaemia is graded by blast percentage and cytogenetics.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. Diseases of White Blood Cells and Transfusion Medicine

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which transfusion reaction presents with fever, loin pain, haemoglobinuria and hypotension within minutes of starting a unit?
options: Acute haemolytic reaction from ABO incompatibility
questions.concept: It is almost always a clerical error, so the transfusion is stopped immediately, the unit and patient identity rechecked, and support given for disseminated intravascular coagulation and renal failure.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. Diseases of White Blood Cells and Transfusion Medicine

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which blood product is indicated to replace fibrinogen specifically?
questions.concept: Cryoprecipitate is concentrated in fibrinogen, factor VIII, von Willebrand factor and factor XIII, so it corrects hypofibrinogenaemia in far less volume than plasma.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. Diseases of White Blood Cells and Transfusion Medicine

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which finding indicates aplastic anaemia rather than myelodysplasia in a patient with pancytopenia?
options: A hypocellular marrow replaced by fat with no dysplasia and no excess blasts
questions.concept: The distinction matters because immunosuppression and transplantation treat aplasia whereas hypomethylating agents and transplantation are used in myelodysplasia, and hypoplastic myelodysplasia can blur the boundary.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. Diseases of White Blood Cells and Transfusion Medicine

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which transfusion complication presents with acute hypoxaemia and bilateral infiltrates within 6 hours, without volume overload?
options: Transfusion-related acute lung injury, mediated by donor antibody against recipient leucocytes
questions.concept: Distinguishing it from circulatory overload matters because the treatment is supportive rather than diuretic, and it is a leading cause of transfusion-related death.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. Diseases of White Blood Cells and Transfusion Medicine

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Why is irradiated blood used for a patient receiving intrauterine transfusion or for a stem cell transplant recipient?
options: Irradiation inactivates donor lymphocytes and prevents transfusion-associated graft versus host disease
It removes leucocytes to prevent febrile reactions
questions.concept: Leucodepletion reduces febrile reactions, HLA alloimmunisation and cytomegalovirus transmission but does not prevent graft versus host disease, which is why the two processes are not interchangeable.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. Diseases of White Blood Cells and Transfusion Medicine

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which criteria define symptomatic multiple myeloma requiring treatment?
options: Clonal plasma cells with hypercalcaemia, renal impairment, anaemia or bone lesions, or a defined biomarker of malignancy
questions.concept: The addition of biomarkers such as 60 percent marrow plasma cells, a light chain ratio above 100 or more than one focal lesion on MRI allows treatment before end-organ damage occurs.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. Diseases of White Blood Cells

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which myeloproliferative neoplasm is defined by the JAK2 V617F mutation with a raised haematocrit and a low erythropoietin?
questions.concept: A low erythropoietin distinguishes it from secondary polycythaemia, and treatment with venesection and low-dose aspirin, with hydroxyurea in high-risk patients, prevents thrombosis.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. Diseases of White Blood Cells

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which finding on blood film suggests primary myelofibrosis?
options: Teardrop poikilocytes with a leucoerythroblastic picture and massive splenomegaly
questions.concept: Marrow fibrosis with extramedullary haemopoiesis produces the film changes, and a dry tap on aspiration with trephine biopsy showing fibrosis confirms it.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. Diseases of White Blood Cells

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which renal lesion is characteristic of multiple myeloma, and by what mechanism?
options: Light chain cast nephropathy, with tubular obstruction and direct tubular toxicity
questions.concept: Because free light chains are filtered and toxic to tubules, urine dipstick for albumin is often negative while total protein is high, so light chain quantification is needed rather than dipstick alone.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. Diseases of White Blood Cells

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which plasma cell disorder presents with a monoclonal IgM, hyperviscosity and lymphadenopathy but without lytic bone lesions?
questions.concept: The large pentameric IgM raises plasma viscosity causing visual disturbance and neurological symptoms, treated urgently by plasmapheresis, and lytic lesions are characteristically absent.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. Diseases of White Blood Cells

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Why does a patient with essential thrombocythaemia bleed as well as thrombose despite a very high platelet count?
options: The platelets are qualitatively abnormal and extreme counts can cause an acquired von Willebrand syndrome by adsorbing the factor
Platelet count is irrelevant to function
questions.concept: This is why aspirin must be used cautiously at very high counts and why cytoreduction rather than antiplatelet therapy alone is used to reduce both risks.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. Diseases of White Blood Cells

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Renal: tubulointerstitial, cystic disease, renal tumours
questions.stem: Which inherited cystic kidney disease is autosomal dominant, presents in adulthood and is associated with berry aneurysms?
options: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease from PKD1 or PKD2 mutation
questions.concept: Extrarenal features include hepatic cysts, mitral valve prolapse, colonic diverticula and intracranial aneurysm, and tolvaptan slows the decline in function in rapidly progressive disease.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. The Kidney

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Renal: tubulointerstitial, cystic disease, renal tumours
questions.stem: Which renal tumour arises from the proximal tubular epithelium, shows clear cells and is associated with VHL inactivation?
questions.concept: The classic triad of haematuria, flank pain and a mass is now uncommon because most are found incidentally, and paraneoplastic polycythaemia, hypercalcaemia and Stauffer syndrome may occur.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. The Kidney

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Renal: tubulointerstitial, cystic disease, renal tumours
questions.stem: Which renal tumour of childhood shows a triphasic blastemal, epithelial and stromal pattern?
questions.concept: It is associated with WT1 mutations in the WAGR and Denys-Drash syndromes and with WT2 in Beckwith-Wiedemann, and biopsy is avoided to prevent upstaging.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. The Kidney

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Renal: tubulointerstitial, cystic disease, renal tumours
questions.stem: Which pattern of renal injury follows chronic analgesic abuse, and what is its hallmark?
options: Chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis with papillary necrosis
questions.concept: Diabetes, sickle cell disease and obstruction with infection are the other classic causes of papillary necrosis, and the sloughed papilla may cause colic and be seen in the urine.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. The Kidney

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Renal: tubulointerstitial, cystic disease, renal tumours
questions.stem: Which finding distinguishes acute tubular necrosis from prerenal azotaemia on urine analysis?
options: Muddy brown granular casts with a fractional excretion of sodium above 2 percent and a low urine osmolality
Bland urine with a fractional excretion below 1 percent
questions.concept: Because injured tubules can neither reabsorb sodium nor concentrate urine, these indices separate the two, though diuretics and chronic kidney disease confound them.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. The Kidney

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Renal: tubulointerstitial, cystic disease, renal tumours
questions.stem: Why does reflux nephropathy cause hypertension and progressive renal failure years after the childhood infections have ceased?
options: Coarse cortical scarring over deformed calyces reduces nephron mass, and hyperfiltration in the remainder drives progressive glomerulosclerosis
Reflux continues into adulthood in all cases
questions.concept: This is the same final common pathway seen in any cause of reduced nephron number, which is why blood pressure control and renin-angiotensin blockade slow progression.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. The Kidney

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which histological change defines the blister of pemphigus vulgaris?
options: Suprabasal intraepidermal acantholysis with a row of tombstones basal layer
questions.concept: Antibodies to desmoglein 3 break cell-cell adhesion so the blister is flaccid and Nikolsky positive, whereas bullous pemphigoid gives tense subepidermal blisters with hemidesmosomal antibodies.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. The Skin

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which feature on histology of a melanocytic lesion most strongly indicates melanoma?
options: Asymmetry with poor circumscription, upward migration of atypical melanocytes and mitoses in the dermal component
questions.concept: Breslow thickness measured from the granular layer to the deepest tumour cell remains the single most important prognostic factor, with ulceration and mitotic rate adding independently.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. The Skin

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which skin malignancy shows peripheral palisading of basaloid cells with retraction artefact and almost never metastasises?
questions.concept: Its local destructiveness rather than metastatic potential determines management, and the sun-exposed head and neck with a rolled pearly edge and telangiectasia is the typical presentation.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. The Skin

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which precursor lesion progresses to invasive squamous cell carcinoma of the skin, and what defines the transition?
options: Actinic keratosis progressing through Bowen disease, with invasion through the basement membrane defining carcinoma
questions.concept: Because the whole sun-damaged field carries risk, field treatment with topical agents or photodynamic therapy is used alongside excision of individual lesions.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. The Skin

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which melanoma subtype has the best prognosis stage for stage because of its long horizontal growth phase?
questions.concept: Nodular melanoma lacks a radial growth phase so it invades early and presents at greater thickness, which explains its worse outcome despite a shorter history.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. The Skin

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Why is a mutation in BRAF clinically important in melanoma?
options: About half of cutaneous melanomas carry a V600E mutation that is targetable with BRAF and MEK inhibitors
It confers a better prognosis without treatment
questions.concept: Because checkpoint inhibition is also highly effective, molecular testing at diagnosis of advanced disease determines whether targeted therapy or immunotherapy is used first.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e, Ch. The Skin
